title: The Langlands Philosophy
description: A unifying conjecture between number theory, harmonic analysis, and representation theory

concepts.title: Langlands' 1967 Letter to Weil
concepts.contentHtml:
In January 1967 a 30-year-old Robert Langlands wrote a 17-page handwritten letter to André Weil sketching what he called 'a possibility' — a vast web of conjectures relating automorphic representations of reductive groups G over global fields to Galois representations of the absolute Galois group Gal(F̄/F). The letter, prefaced with the famous disclaimer 'If you are willing to read it as pure speculation I would appreciate that; if not — I am sure you have a waste basket handy', became the seed of what is now called the Langlands program.

The core slogan: every n-dimensional Galois representation should correspond to a cuspidal automorphic representation of GL_n, with matching L-functions. More generally, for any reductive group G, automorphic forms on G(\mathbb{A}_F) should be parametrized by homomorphisms from the Weil-Deligne or Langlands group into the Langlands dual group {}^L G.

This single organizing principle subsumes class field theory (the case n=1), the modularity of elliptic curves (the case n=2), Artin's conjecture, the Shimura-Taniyama conjecture, and a long list of identities of L-functions. It is, by consensus, one of the two or three deepest organizing visions in modern mathematics.

concepts.title: Why It Matters: Reciprocity Beyond Class Field Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Classical class field theory, developed by Takagi, Artin, and Chevalley between 1920 and 1950, classifies abelian extensions of a number field F via the idele class group: \mathrm{Gal}(F^{ab}/F) \cong F^\times \backslash \mathbb{A}_F^\times / (\text{connected component}). This is a one-dimensional case of Langlands — GL_1-automorphic characters correspond to one-dimensional Galois reps.

The Langlands program asks: what about non-abelian extensions? Direct generalization fails — the Galois group of F̄/F is profinite and topologically wild. Langlands's bet was that the right replacement for 'characters of the Galois group' is automorphic representations, infinite-dimensional representations of adelic groups whose decomposition is governed by harmonic analysis.

Concrete consequences: Artin's conjecture on holomorphy of L-functions, the Sato-Tate distribution of Frobenius eigenvalues, the Ramanujan-Petersson bounds, and ultimately Fermat's Last Theorem (via modularity). Each is a fragment of one master correspondence. Crucially, the Langlands philosophy is predictive: it tells you what theorems should be true and what their L-functions should look like, even when proofs remain out of reach.

concepts.title: The Function Field Analogy
concepts.contentHtml:
Number fields like \mathbb{Q} and function fields like \mathbb{F}_q(T) share an extraordinary structural parallel: both are global fields, both have rings of integers, ideles, and Galois groups. André Weil exploited this analogy throughout his career; the Langlands program inherits it as a guiding principle.

Over function fields, geometry can be brought to bear. A curve X over \mathbb{F}_q plays the role of \mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}, and \ell-adic sheaves on X play the role of Galois representations. Vladimir Drinfeld proved Langlands for GL_2 over function fields in his 1978 thesis using shtukas, a geometric object encoding modifications of vector bundles. Laurent Lafforgue extended this to all GL_n in 2002, earning a Fields Medal.

Function-field Langlands is not just an analogy — it is, in many ways, the cleaner theory, where geometric methods (étale cohomology, perverse sheaves, the geometric Satake equivalence) are immediately available. Insights from the function-field side regularly feed back into number-field problems. The 2018 Fields Medal to Akshay Venkatesh and the 2024 announcement of the geometric Langlands proof are direct descendants of this transfer.

title: Automorphic Forms and Representations
description: From modular forms on the upper half-plane to representations of GL_2(A)

concepts.title: Holomorphic and Maass Forms
concepts.contentHtml:
A holomorphic modular form of weight k for SL_2(\mathbb{Z}) is a holomorphic function f : \mathbb{H} \to \mathbb{C} on the upper half-plane satisfying f((az+b)/(cz+d)) = (cz+d)^k f(z) for all \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} \in SL_2(\mathbb{Z}), with controlled growth at the cusp. Examples: Eisenstein series E_k, the discriminant \Delta(z) = q\prod(1-q^n)^{24} of weight 12.

Maass forms, introduced by Hans Maass in 1949, are real-analytic rather than holomorphic. They are eigenfunctions of the hyperbolic Laplacian \Delta = -y^2(\partial_x^2 + \partial_y^2) with eigenvalue \lambda = \tfrac{1}{4} + r^2 and the same modular invariance (weight zero). They have no classical analog in the holomorphic theory, yet they are equally automorphic and contribute their own L-functions.

Both objects fit into a single representation-theoretic picture once we move to the adelic setting. Holomorphic forms correspond to representations whose archimedean component is a discrete-series rep D_k of GL_2(\mathbb{R}); Maass forms correspond to principal-series reps with continuous parameter r. The Selberg eigenvalue conjecture \lambda \geq 1/4 on congruence subgroups is a Ramanujan bound for Maass forms — still open in full generality.

concepts.title: Adeles, Strong Approximation, and GL_2(A)
concepts.contentHtml:
The ring of adeles \mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}} = \mathbb{R} \times \prod'_p \mathbb{Q}_p is the restricted product over all places, including the archimedean one. It bundles all completions of \mathbb{Q} into a single locally compact topological ring on which \mathbb{Q} sits diagonally as a discrete cocompact subring (modulo \widehat{\mathbb{Z}}). Haar measure exists; Fourier analysis works.

The adelic group GL_2(\mathbb{A}) contains GL_2(\mathbb{Q}) as a discrete subgroup. Strong approximation for SL_2 (Kneser, Platonov) combined with class number 1 for \mathbb{Q} implies GL_2(\mathbb{Q}) \backslash GL_2(\mathbb{A}) / K_f Z(\mathbb{R})^\circ \cong \Gamma_0(N) \backslash \mathbb{H} when K_f = \prod_p K_p is a level subgroup. Classical modular curves and the adelic double-coset space are the same object; modular forms become functions on this double coset space, with the adelic group acting by right translation.

An automorphic representation is an irreducible subquotient of L^2(GL_2(\mathbb{Q}) Z(\mathbb{A}) \backslash GL_2(\mathbb{A})). By the tensor product theorem (Flath, after Jacquet-Langlands 1970), each such \pi factors as a restricted tensor product \pi = \bigotimes'_v \pi_v over local components. Each \pi_v is an admissible irreducible representation of GL_2(\mathbb{Q}_v) — a purely local object that classical theory hides from view.

concepts.title: Cuspidal Forms and Eisenstein Series
concepts.contentHtml:
The space of automorphic forms decomposes into a cuspidal part and a continuous (Eisenstein) part: L^2 = L^2_{\mathrm{cusp}} \oplus L^2_{\mathrm{Eis}} \oplus L^2_{\mathrm{res}}. Cuspidal forms vanish at every cusp — equivalently, their constant Fourier coefficient along every parabolic is zero. They form the discrete spectrum after quotienting by residues.

Eisenstein series E(g, s) = \sum_{\gamma \in B(\mathbb{Q}) \backslash GL_2(\mathbb{Q})} f_s(\gamma g) furnish the continuous spectrum. They depend meromorphically on s and possess a functional equation E(g, s) \leftrightarrow E(g, 1-s) via the intertwining operator. Selberg's analytic continuation of Eisenstein series is one of the technical pillars of the theory; Langlands later gave the general construction for arbitrary parabolics in his 1976 book.

The cuspidal spectrum is where the deepest arithmetic lives. By Gelfand-Piatetski-Shapiro multiplicity one, each cuspidal automorphic representation of GL_n appears at most once in L^2_{\mathrm{cusp}} — the analog of saying a number is determined by its prime factorization. This rigidity makes \pi behave like a true 'object' rather than just a vector in some Hilbert space, and it is what allows L-function comparisons to make sense globally.
mathExpressions: E(g, s) = \sum_{\gamma \in B(\mathbb{Q})\backslash G(\mathbb{Q})} f_s(\gamma g)

title: L-functions and Functional Equations
description: Hecke's adelic synthesis, automorphic L-functions, and the conjectured continuation

concepts.title: From Hecke to Tate
concepts.contentHtml:
Erich Hecke (1936) attached an L-function L(s, f) = \sum a_n n^{-s} to a modular form f = \sum a_n q^n, proved its Euler product L(s, f) = \prod_p (1 - a_p p^{-s} + p^{k-1-2s})^{-1} for Hecke eigenforms, and established its analytic continuation and functional equation by Mellin-transforming f against a theta-style integral.

John Tate's 1950 thesis recast Hecke's argument adelically. To a Hecke character \chi : \mathbb{Q}^\times \backslash \mathbb{A}^\times \to \mathbb{C}^\times and a Schwartz function \Phi on \mathbb{A}, Tate defined Z(\Phi, \chi, s) = \int_{\mathbb{A}^\times} \Phi(x) \chi(x) |x|^s \, d^\times x. The Poisson summation formula on \mathbb{A}/\mathbb{Q} immediately gives the functional equation Z(\Phi, \chi, s) = Z(\widehat{\Phi}, \chi^{-1}, 1-s) — a single line replacing pages of classical computation.

Tate's thesis is the template for everything in automorphic L-functions: each L(s, \pi) is built as an integral of a matrix coefficient of \pi against a test function, and the functional equation comes from a global symmetry (Poisson summation, or its higher analogs from automorphic kernels). Fundamental insight: L-functions are not auxiliary tools — they are images of automorphic representations under a precise integral transform.

concepts.title: Automorphic L-functions and Euler Products
concepts.contentHtml:
To an automorphic representation \pi = \otimes' \pi_v of GL_n(\mathbb{A}) and a finite-dimensional representation r : {}^L G \to GL_N(\mathbb{C}) of the Langlands dual, Langlands attaches a global L-function as an Euler product over places: L(s, \pi, r) = \prod_v L_v(s, \pi_v, r). At unramified places v, the local factor is L_v(s, \pi_v, r) = \det(1 - r(\mathrm{Sat}(\pi_v)) q_v^{-s})^{-1}, where \mathrm{Sat}(\pi_v) \in {}^L G is the Satake parameter — a semisimple conjugacy class encoding \pi_v's Hecke eigenvalues.

For \pi on GL_n and r = \mathrm{std} the standard n-dimensional rep, this recovers the principal L-function L(s, \pi). For r = \mathrm{Sym}^k we get symmetric power L-functions, central to Sato-Tate. For two reps \pi_1 on GL_n, \pi_2 on GL_m, the Rankin-Selberg L-function L(s, \pi_1 \times \pi_2) uses r = \mathrm{std} \otimes \mathrm{std}.

Each automorphic L-function is conjectured to satisfy a functional equation \Lambda(s, \pi, r) = \varepsilon(s, \pi, r)\Lambda(1-s, \pi^\vee, r) where \Lambda includes archimedean Gamma factors. Generalized Ramanujan conjectures that all Satake parameters are unitary, giving uniform bounds |\alpha_v| = 1. Both the functional equation and Ramanujan are theorems for GL_n-cuspidal reps in many cases, but open in full generality beyond.
mathExpressions: L(s, \pi, r) = \prod_v L_v(s, \pi_v, r) = \prod_v \det(1 - r(A_{\pi_v}) q_v^{-s})^{-1}

concepts.title: Functoriality and the Converse Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
Langlands functoriality is the conjecture that any homomorphism of L-groups \rho : {}^L H \to {}^L G should induce a transfer of automorphic representations \pi_H \rightsquigarrow \pi_G = \rho_*(\pi_H) matching L-functions: L(s, \pi_H, r \circ \rho) = L(s, \pi_G, r). Specializations include base change, automorphic induction, symmetric power lifts \mathrm{Sym}^k : GL_2 \to GL_{k+1}, and Langlands-Rapoport descents.

Functoriality is staggeringly powerful: it would imply Artin's conjecture, Sato-Tate, the holomorphy of all motivic L-functions, and the Generalized Ramanujan Conjecture. Known cases include cyclic base change (Arthur-Clozel 1989), Rankin-Selberg (Jacquet-Piatetski-Shapiro-Shalika), \mathrm{Sym}^2 (Gelbart-Jacquet 1978), \mathrm{Sym}^3, \mathrm{Sym}^4 for GL_2 (Kim-Shahidi 2002), and recently \mathrm{Sym}^k for all k on holomorphic forms (Newton-Thorne 2021).

Converse theorems, originating with Hecke and refined by Weil and Cogdell-Piatetski-Shapiro, run the reverse: if a Dirichlet series and 'enough' twists by Rankin-Selberg with GL_m share the expected functional equations, then it is automorphic. They are the bridge from analytic data to representations and a central tool in establishing functoriality cases.

title: Galois Representations
description: Tate modules, Frobenius eigenvalues, and the arithmetic side of the correspondence

concepts.title: Tate Modules of Elliptic Curves
concepts.contentHtml:
For an elliptic curve E/\mathbb{Q} and a prime \ell, the \ell^n-torsion E[\ell^n](\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \cong (\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n)^2 carries a continuous action of G_{\mathbb{Q}} = \mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q}). The inverse limit T_\ell E = \varprojlim E[\ell^n] \cong \mathbb{Z}_\ell^2 is the Tate module; tensoring with \mathbb{Q}_\ell gives a 2-dimensional \ell-adic Galois representation \rho_{E, \ell} : G_{\mathbb{Q}} \to GL_2(\mathbb{Q}_\ell).

This representation is unramified at every prime p of good reduction p \nmid \ell N. At such p, the Frobenius element \mathrm{Frob}_p acts with characteristic polynomial X^2 - a_p X + p, where a_p = p + 1 - \#E(\mathbb{F}_p). The eigenvalues \alpha_p, \beta_p satisfy \alpha_p \beta_p = p and |\alpha_p| = |\beta_p| = \sqrt{p} by the Hasse bound — the elliptic-curve case of the Weil conjectures.

The numbers a_p are the same Frobenius traces that appear as Hecke eigenvalues in modular forms. Modularity says these two sources of a_p coincide: there is a weight-2 cusp form f_E of level N = \mathrm{cond}(E) with a_p(f_E) = a_p(E) for all p. This is the bridge between Galois reps and automorphic reps in its most concrete form.

concepts.title: Galois Representations from Modular Forms
concepts.contentHtml:
To a normalized cuspidal Hecke eigenform f = \sum a_n q^n \in S_k(\Gamma_0(N)), Eichler-Shimura (weight 2) and then Deligne (1971, weights k \geq 2) attached a 2-dimensional \ell-adic Galois representation \rho_{f, \ell} : G_{\mathbb{Q}} \to GL_2(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell). The construction uses étale cohomology of modular curves (or, for k \geq 3, of Kuga-Sato varieties); \rho_{f, \ell} appears as a quotient of H^1_{\mathrm{et}}(X_0(N)_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}, \mathbb{Q}_\ell).

The defining property: at unramified primes p \nmid N\ell, \mathrm{tr}\,\rho_{f, \ell}(\mathrm{Frob}_p) = a_p and \det \rho_{f, \ell}(\mathrm{Frob}_p) = p^{k-1} \chi(p), where \chi is the nebentypus. The Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture |a_p| \leq 2 p^{(k-1)/2} — proved for holomorphic forms by Deligne via the Weil conjectures (1974) — is exactly the statement that Frobenius eigenvalues have absolute value p^{(k-1)/2}.

Even Maass forms are conjectured to give Galois representations, but the construction is far harder because Maass forms are not realized in the cohomology of any algebraic variety. For weight-1 holomorphic forms, the Galois rep is finite-image (Deligne-Serre), and the Artin conjecture follows. The general Maass case remains essentially open, illustrating that Langlands beyond cohomological reach is genuinely deeper terrain.

concepts.title: Fontaine-Mazur and Geometricity
concepts.contentHtml:
Not every \ell-adic Galois representation comes from geometry. The Fontaine-Mazur conjecture (1995) characterizes those that should: an irreducible \ell-adic representation \rho : G_{\mathbb{Q}} \to GL_n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell) arises as a subquotient of H^i_{\mathrm{et}}(X_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}, \mathbb{Q}_\ell) for some smooth projective X/\mathbb{Q} if and only if it is unramified outside a finite set and de Rham at \ell.

The p-adic Hodge condition 'de Rham' (Fontaine 1980s) is a delicate local condition at \ell: a representation is de Rham iff D_{\mathrm{dR}}(\rho) := (\rho \otimes B_{\mathrm{dR}})^{G_{\mathbb{Q}_\ell}} has dimension n. It is the \ell-adic analog of being motivic — a local-monodromy constraint matching what cohomology provides.

Combining Fontaine-Mazur with the Langlands philosophy yields the modern reciprocity vision: every irreducible Galois representation that is geometric (= unramified outside finitely many primes and de Rham at \ell) corresponds to a cuspidal automorphic representation of GL_n(\mathbb{A}) with matching L-function. The Wiles modularity proof, Khare-Wintenberger's proof of Serre's conjecture (2008), and the Calegari-Geraghty machinery for ten-dimensional reps are all instances of this big picture being made into theorems.

title: Modularity and Wiles-Taylor
description: From Frey-Hellegouarch to the proof of Fermat via R = T

concepts.title: The Shimura-Taniyama Conjecture
concepts.contentHtml:
Goro Shimura and Yutaka Taniyama, in conversations at the 1955 Tokyo-Nikko symposium, conjectured that every elliptic curve E/\mathbb{Q} is modular: there exists a weight-2 newform f \in S_2(\Gamma_0(N)) with L(s, E) = L(s, f), where N = \mathrm{cond}(E). Equivalently, \rho_{E, \ell} \cong \rho_{f, \ell}; equivalently, there is a non-constant map X_0(N) \to E defined over \mathbb{Q}.

Frey (1986) and Serre (1987) noticed that a hypothetical solution a^p + b^p = c^p to Fermat's equation would produce a semistable elliptic curve E_{a,b,c}: y^2 = x(x-a^p)(x+b^p) whose Galois representation would have absurdly small ramification — it would violate Serre's conjecture on modular Galois representations, which Ribet (1990) proved sufficient: 'epsilon' lowers level so far that no modular form can exist. Conclusion: modularity of E_{a,b,c} + Ribet's theorem \Rightarrow Fermat.

By 1993 the implication was airtight; only modularity for the relevant semistable curves remained. The conjecture, once 'inaccessible', had been turned into the bottleneck of the most famous open problem in mathematics.
mathExpressions: L(s, E) = L(s, f), \quad f \in S_2(\Gamma_0(N)), \; N = \mathrm{cond}(E)

concepts.title: Wiles, Taylor, and R = T
concepts.contentHtml:
Andrew Wiles announced in June 1993 a proof of modularity for semistable elliptic curves over \mathbb{Q}. His strategy: prove that a certain universal deformation ring R, parameterizing deformations of the residual mod-\ell Galois representation \bar\rho_{E, \ell}, is isomorphic to a Hecke algebra T acting on the relevant space of modular forms. The slogan R = T compresses the entire approach.

A gap discovered in late 1993 took fourteen months to repair. Wiles, working with Richard Taylor, replaced the original Euler-system argument with a 'patching' construction that became the Taylor-Wiles method. The two papers — Wiles' Modular Elliptic Curves and Fermat's Last Theorem (Annals 1995, 109 pages) and Taylor-Wiles' Ring-Theoretic Properties of Certain Hecke Algebras — proved modularity of all semistable E/\mathbb{Q}, more than enough for Fermat.

Breuil, Conrad, Diamond, and Taylor extended the result to all elliptic curves over \mathbb{Q} in 2001, completing the original Shimura-Taniyama conjecture in full. The Taylor-Wiles patching method was generalized by Kisin, Calegari-Geraghty, and others to handle higher-dimensional and higher-rank situations — it remains the most powerful technique for proving modularity-style theorems today.

concepts.title: After Wiles: Sato-Tate, Serre, and Beyond
concepts.contentHtml:
Modularity is the seed crystal for a cascade of subsequent theorems. The Sato-Tate conjecture — that for a non-CM elliptic curve, the normalized Frobenius angles \theta_p \in [0, \pi] defined by a_p / 2\sqrt{p} = \cos\theta_p equidistribute according to (2/\pi)\sin^2\theta\, d\theta, the spectral measure of SU(2) — was settled by Clozel-Harris-Shepherd-Barron-Taylor (2008) using potential automorphy of all symmetric powers \mathrm{Sym}^k(\rho_{E, \ell}). The argument required modularity lifting for GL_n, n arbitrary, vastly generalizing the original Wiles strategy.

Serre's modularity conjecture on irreducible odd 2-dimensional mod-\ell representations \bar\rho : G_{\mathbb{Q}} \to GL_2(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_\ell) was proved by Khare-Wintenberger (2008-2009) and Kisin, completing the residual side of the picture and implying Artin's conjecture for odd two-dimensional representations. The proof bootstraps via successive level/weight reductions and an inductive use of modularity lifting.

Modern modularity lifting theorems handle: Hilbert modular forms (Skinner-Wiles, Kisin), totally real fields (Taylor and others: every elliptic curve over a totally real field is potentially modular), imaginary quadratic fields (Allen-Calegari-Caraiani-Gee-Helm-Le Hung-Newton-Scholze-Taylor-Thorne, 2023), and abelian surfaces (Boxer-Calegari-Gee-Pilloni 2021). Each follows the R = T blueprint with deeper input from p-adic Hodge theory.
mathExpressions: \text{All } E/F \;\text{(totally real $F$)} \;\text{are potentially modular} \quad \text{(Taylor et al.)}

title: Local Langlands
description: GL_n over local fields, Harris-Taylor, and Langlands parameters

concepts.title: Local Fields and the Weil-Deligne Group
concepts.contentHtml:
A local field F is the completion of a global field at a place: \mathbb{R}, \mathbb{C}, the p-adic fields \mathbb{Q}_p and finite extensions, or local function fields \mathbb{F}_q((t)). Each carries an absolute Galois group G_F with a rich tower of subgroups: inertia I_F, wild inertia P_F \subset I_F, and the quotient G_F/I_F = \widehat{\mathbb{Z}} generated by Frobenius.

For local Langlands, the right object is not G_F itself but the Weil group W_F — a dense subgroup with discrete Frobenius — and its enrichment, the Weil-Deligne group {}^L W_F = W_F \times SL_2(\mathbb{C}) (or W_F \ltimes \mathbb{C} with monodromy). The extra SL_2 factor packages the unipotent monodromy that arises from non-semisimple representations and is essential to capture all irreducible admissible reps on the automorphic side.

The key dichotomy: representations of G_F that are continuous in the natural \ell-adic topology are tamer than they look, and the Weil-Deligne formalism makes this precise. Grothendieck's monodromy theorem: every continuous \rho : G_F \to GL_n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell) arises from a Weil-Deligne representation (r, N) with r semisimple on inertia and N nilpotent. This is what Galois reps look like locally.

concepts.title: The Local Langlands Correspondence for GL_n
concepts.contentHtml:
The local Langlands correspondence (LLC) for GL_n is a bijection: \{\text{irreducible smooth admissible reps of } GL_n(F)\}/\!\sim \;\longleftrightarrow\; \{\text{$n$-dim Frobenius-semisimple WD reps of } W_F\}/\!\sim. The bijection is uniquely characterized by compatibility with class field theory (the case n=1), preservation of L- and \varepsilon-factors of pairs, and twists by characters.

For F = \mathbb{R} or \mathbb{C}, this is Langlands' own 1973 classification of admissible representations of real reductive groups — every irreducible admissible rep of GL_n(\mathbb{R}) is parametrized by a homomorphism W_{\mathbb{R}} \to GL_n(\mathbb{C}). For non-archimedean F, the case n=2 was handled by Kutzko (1980); the general case was proved by Harris and Taylor (2001) using the cohomology of Shimura varieties of unitary type, and reproved by Henniart (2000) by purely local methods using \varepsilon-factors and a numerical match.

Scholze (2013) gave a third proof using perfectoid spaces and the Lubin-Tate tower. The Harris-Taylor proof, beyond LLC itself, established the existence of Galois representations attached to many automorphic representations of GL_n — input that fed back into Sato-Tate and the modularity-lifting program for higher rank.

concepts.title: L-packets and Beyond GL_n
concepts.contentHtml:
For a general reductive group G/F, the local Langlands correspondence is no longer a bijection. Instead, Langlands parameters \phi : W_F \times SL_2(\mathbb{C}) \to {}^L G(\mathbb{C}) are conjectured to parametrize L-packets — finite sets \Pi_\phi of irreducible reps. Within a packet, individual reps are distinguished by an internal parameter \rho \in \widehat{S_\phi}, where S_\phi is the centralizer-component group of \phi.

Internal structure of L-packets has been settled in many cases. Arthur classified discrete spectrum of classical groups (orthogonal/symplectic) in 2013, later extended by Mok to unitary groups. The local Langlands for general reductive groups remains an active field; recent breakthroughs include Fargues-Scholze's geometric construction of the local Langlands correspondence (2021) using the stack \mathrm{Bun}_G on the Fargues-Fontaine curve, giving a uniform framework that subsumes earlier ad hoc proofs.

Why packets at all? On the dual side, conjugacy classes of parameters live in {}^L G, whereas the automorphic side detects representations of G(F). The fibers of the natural map between these — the L-packets — encode multiplicities, endoscopic transfers, and the failure of strong multiplicity one beyond GL_n. Without packets, the most basic identities of automorphic L-functions don't make sense.

title: Geometric Langlands
description: Sheaves, D-modules, and the 2024 proof of geometric Langlands

concepts.title: Drinfeld and the Geometric Reformulation
concepts.contentHtml:
For a smooth projective curve X over \mathbb{F}_q or \mathbb{C}, geometric Langlands replaces automorphic forms with sheaves on the moduli stack \mathrm{Bun}_G(X) of G-bundles on X. The conjecture: there is an equivalence of categories D(\mathrm{Bun}_G(X)) \;\simeq\; \mathrm{QCoh}(\mathrm{LocSys}_{{}^L G}(X)) between (\ell-adic / D-module) sheaves on \mathrm{Bun}_G and quasi-coherent sheaves on the moduli of {}^L G-local systems.

This is an upgrade, not a metaphor. Functions become sheaves; eigenfunctions of Hecke operators become Hecke eigensheaves; Galois representations become local systems. Drinfeld in the late 1970s realized that proving function-field Langlands amounted to constructing such Hecke eigensheaves. His invention of shtukas — a moduli space combining a vector bundle with a Frobenius-twisted modification — enabled this, and led to his proof of GL_2 (1978) and Lafforgue's proof of GL_n (2002, Fields Medal).

Over \mathbb{C}, the geometric formulation is purely algebraic-geometric and category-theoretic. There is no Frobenius, but the structure of \mathrm{Bun}_G and the Hecke action remain. This is where 'geometric Langlands' in the contemporary sense lives: a categorified version of the global function-field correspondence with no number theory in sight, but extraordinary depth.

concepts.title: Beilinson-Drinfeld and the Hecke Functor
concepts.contentHtml:
Beilinson-Drinfeld's 1990s manuscripts gave the first systematic construction of Hecke eigensheaves over \mathbb{C}, building on the geometric Satake equivalence: \mathrm{Perv}(\mathrm{Gr}_G) \simeq \mathrm{Rep}({}^L G) identifying perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian with finite-dimensional representations of the Langlands dual. This is a categorified version of the unramified local Langlands and is the engine behind global geometric statements.

For an {}^L G-local system \sigma on X, the conjectured Hecke eigensheaf \mathcal{F}_\sigma on \mathrm{Bun}_G satisfies H_V(\mathcal{F}_\sigma) \simeq V_\sigma \boxtimes \mathcal{F}_\sigma for every V \in \mathrm{Rep}({}^L G), where H_V is the Hecke functor labeled by V. Constructing \mathcal{F}_\sigma for arbitrary \sigma was, for two decades, the central open problem of geometric Langlands.

Beilinson-Drinfeld solved the case where \sigma is an oper — a local system equipped with extra structure giving a unique 'origin' — by constructing eigensheaves as D-modules on \mathrm{Bun}_G whose support encodes the Hitchin integrable system. This connected geometric Langlands to Hitchin's integrable system, conformal blocks, and quantum field theory (Kapustin-Witten), revealing the program as a node in a much larger network of dualities.

concepts.title: The 2024 Proof of Geometric Langlands
concepts.contentHtml:
In May 2024, a team led by Dennis Gaitsgory and including Sam Raskin, Dario Beraldo, Lin Chen, Justin Campbell, Joakim Færgeman, Kevin Lin, and Nick Rozenblyum announced a proof of the geometric Langlands conjecture for any reductive group G over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. The argument runs to roughly 800 pages across five papers and rests on two decades of program-building by Gaitsgory and collaborators.

The proof's centerpiece is the spectral decomposition of D(\mathrm{Bun}_G) over \mathrm{LocSys}_{{}^L G}, achieved using derived algebraic geometry (Lurie), factorization categories (Beilinson-Drinfeld), the Whittaker model on the geometric side, and a delicate fiber-by-fiber analysis using temperedness conditions. The result is the categorical equivalence D(\mathrm{Bun}_G) \simeq \mathrm{IndCoh}_{\mathcal{N}}(\mathrm{LocSys}_{{}^L G}) — with the modification 'IndCoh with nilpotent singular support' on the spectral side, a refinement first conjectured by Arinkin-Gaitsgory.

Implications run in many directions: connections to the Kapustin-Witten twist of \mathcal{N}=4 super-Yang-Mills, to the Fargues-Scholze local geometric Langlands, and to arithmetic geometric Langlands over function fields (still open in the categorical form). Geometric Langlands is now a theorem; the program now turns to extending the methods to ramified cases, to other groups, and back across the function-field/number-field bridge to attack the original arithmetic conjectures Langlands wrote down in 1967.
